title: Trump Reinstates Schedule F, Strips Civil Service Protections from Senior Federal Employees
description_short: Trump Reinstates Schedule F, Strips Civil Service Protections from Senior Federal Employees
description_medium: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump reinstated the 2020 Schedule F framework by executive order, renaming it Schedule Policy/Career. The order covered positions the administration classifies as confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating. It directed agencies to identify positions for the new schedule and removed specified adverse-action procedures for covered jobs. The order created a route for reclassification; it did not mean every potentially covered employee had already lost protections.
description_long: On January 21, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order reinstating the 2020 Schedule F framework under the name Schedule Policy/Career. It applies to career positions described as confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating, and directs agencies to identify positions for inclusion. The order also changes the procedures available to employees in covered roles when agencies take adverse action. It says those employees need not personally or politically support the president or administration, but must faithfully implement administration policy; failure to do so is grounds for dismissal. The order directs the Office of Personnel Management to issue guidance on additional categories for agencies to consider and tells agencies to review certain workforce policies. These provisions make the classification and dismissal rules the central issue. The executive order sets a process for agencies to identify covered jobs, rather than documenting how many workers were ultimately reclassified or dismissed. Estimates of the number of positions potentially affected should therefore be distinguished from completed personnel changes.

title: Trump Fires AG Jeff Sessions to Install Loyalist Over Mueller Investigation
description_short: Trump Fires AG Jeff Sessions to Install Loyalist Over Mueller Investigation
description_medium: On November 7, 2018, the day after the midterm elections, Donald Trump asked Attorney General Jeff Sessions to resign and named Sessions’s chief of staff, Matthew Whitaker, acting attorney general. Whitaker had publicly criticized the scope of the Mueller investigation, which Sessions had recused himself from overseeing. The appointment prompted questions about who would supervise the Russia probe.
description_long: On November 7, 2018, the day after the midterm elections, Attorney General Jeff Sessions resigned at Donald Trump’s request, and Trump named Matthew Whitaker, Sessions’s chief of staff, as acting attorney general. Sessions had recused himself from the Russia investigation. Whitaker had publicly criticized the scope of the Mueller probe and suggested ways it could be limited, so his appointment placed oversight of the investigation under an official who had questioned its reach. The change drew immediate objections from Democrats, who warned that Whitaker should not interfere with the inquiry, and constitutional questions from legal scholars because he had not been confirmed by the Senate for another position. Critics viewed the timing and appointment as a potential threat to the investigation, but the personnel change alone does not establish Trump’s motive or show that Whitaker halted the probe. The event was a change in Justice Department leadership during an active investigation, with the successor’s prior comments and the limits of an acting appointment at the center of the debate.

title: RFK Jr. Says He Plans to Tell CDC to Stop Recommending Community Water Fluoridation
description_short: RFK Jr. Says He Plans to Tell CDC to Stop Recommending Community Water Fluoridation
description_medium: In April 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said he planned to direct the CDC to stop recommending fluoridation of public drinking water and said HHS would convene a task force to reassess the issue. At that point CDC's recommendation had not yet been removed. Major dental and public-health organizations continued to support community fluoridation at recommended levels.
description_long: In April 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said he planned to tell the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to stop recommending community water fluoridation. He also said HHS would convene a task force to reassess the issue. The announcement described a proposed directive and review, not a completed change to CDC guidance: at the time of the report, the agency’s recommendation remained in place. Major dental and public-health organizations continued to support fluoridation at recommended levels. The distinction is important to the event’s scope. Kennedy’s statement placed federal guidance under review, but it did not itself remove the CDC recommendation or establish a change in the water supplied by communities. The report documents what the secretary said he intended to do and the task force he said HHS would convene. It does not report the outcome of that review. The controversy therefore concerned a planned shift in federal public-health advice and the evidence HHS would revisit, rather than a policy change already carried out by the CDC.

title: Trump Pulls US Out of UNESCO
description_short: Trump Pulls US Out of UNESCO
description_medium: On October 12, 2017, the Trump administration announced that the United States would withdraw from UNESCO, the UN agency for education, science, and culture. The State Department cited mounting U.S. arrears, a need for reform, and what it called continuing anti-Israel bias. Israel also announced its intention to leave. The decision renewed a debate over U.S. participation in multilateral institutions.
description_long: On October 12, 2017, the Trump administration announced that the United States would withdraw from UNESCO, the United Nations agency working across education, science, and culture. The State Department gave three stated reasons: mounting U.S. financial arrears, the need for reform, and what it described as continuing anti-Israel bias. Israel announced its own withdrawal on the same day. The U.S. announcement followed an earlier departure under President Ronald Reagan in 1984; the country rejoined UNESCO in 2003. UNESCO’s director-general expressed regret, while critics argued that leaving would reduce U.S. influence in an organization involved in cultural heritage, education, and related international work. The announcement was a decision to end U.S. membership, not an immediate end to every connection with programs associated with the organization. The episode placed the administration’s stated objections alongside concerns about American participation in a multilateral forum and repeated a withdrawal-and-return cycle in U.S. relations with UNESCO.

title: DOJ Freezes Civil Rights Division Litigation Pending Trump Administration Review
description_short: DOJ Freezes Civil Rights Division Litigation Pending Trump Administration Review
description_medium: The Justice Department ordered a halt to new and ongoing Civil Rights Division litigation and settlements while cases were reviewed. The evidence does not support the claim that the entire senior leadership was placed on leave on January 21 or that the division ceased to function.
description_long: On January 22, 2025, Reuters reported that the Justice Department had ordered a pause in new and ongoing Civil Rights Division litigation and settlements while the cases were reviewed. The directive affected the division’s legal work during the administration transition and required pending matters to wait for review before proceeding. A halt on new cases and a pause in cases already underway have different consequences for the division’s docket, but the reported order covered both. The account does not say that the division stopped operating or that every senior leader was placed on leave. Nor does it establish that each matter under review was ultimately abandoned: the directive described a review period, not final outcomes for individual cases. The event was an instruction to suspend litigation and settlement activity while the department reassessed cases inherited from the previous administration. Its immediate documented effect was procedural delay pending review; the report does not establish what disposition followed for each case.

title: Secret Service Pays Trump Properties $1.4M for Rooms Protecting Trump
description_short: Secret Service Pays Trump Properties $1.4M for Rooms Protecting Trump
description_medium: A House Oversight Committee letter based on Secret Service records reported more than $1.4 million in lodging payments to Trump-owned U.S. properties from January 20, 2017, through September 15, 2021. Agents stayed at those properties while protecting Trump and his family. The committee said the records it received were incomplete and raised questions about the rates charged.
description_long: A 2022 House Oversight Committee letter, based on Secret Service records, said the agency spent more than $1.4 million on lodging at Trump-owned U.S. properties between January 20, 2017, and September 15, 2021. Agents needed accommodations while protecting Donald Trump and members of his family at properties that included his clubs and resorts. The committee said the records it received were incomplete, so the total represented documented payments rather than a full accounting. Its inquiry also raised questions about nightly rates; the supplied account says some rooms cost hundreds of dollars per night and that rates were at or above commercial levels. The records establish payments to Trump businesses for lodging connected to protective duties. Those payments brought public security spending into businesses Trump continued to own, prompting scrutiny of their pricing and transparency. The reported sum is the amount spent by the agency, not evidence that the same amount became Trump’s personal profit. The committee’s letter framed the issue as a need to account for charges and missing records.

title: Jared Kushner Tangled with Albanian Mob in Real Estate Deal
description_short: Jared Kushner partnered with alleged Albanian gangsters on a luxury resort project, raising concerns about corruption and ties to organized crime.
description_medium: Jared Kushner’s investment fund pursued luxury development projects on Albania’s Sazan island and near Zvërnec, including land bought with partners connected to a Qatari billionaire’s family. The Nation reported that some land was linked to Artur Shehu, whom the Wall Street Journal described as a suspected gangster. Shehu denies wrongdoing and has not been convicted.
description_long: Jared Kushner’s investment fund, Affinity Partners, pursued luxury hotel projects on Sazan, an island off Albania, and on marshland near Zvërnec. The Nation reported that Affinity worked with members of the family of Qatari billionaire Moutaz Khayyat and that Kushner’s consortium sought to buy land from Artur Shehu. The Wall Street Journal described Shehu as a suspected gangster; The Nation reported that he was arrested in Albania in June on organized-crime charges, which he denies, and that he has not been convicted. The land deal also drew a dispute from Zvërnec villagers, who wrote to Kushner in 2024 claiming that land he was buying from Shehu belonged to them. The article recounts a court finding that a land record had been mistranslated and that a lawyer and archivist were convicted in a related falsified-document case, with the lawyer’s case later retried. These allegations and reported disputes explain the project’s scrutiny; they do not establish that Kushner knew of or participated in criminal conduct.

title: Trump Runs into Roadblocks in Plot to Seize Elections
description_short: Trump Runs into Roadblocks in Plot to Seize Elections
description_medium: As the 2026 midterms approached, the Trump administration faced court losses and legislative resistance to efforts affecting federal election administration. The Independent reported more than 20 Justice Department losses in cases seeking voter data, repeated court blocks of executive orders on mail ballots and voter registration, and no congressional agreement on the SAVE America Act. Trump also left open a host’s suggestion of declaring a national emergency to impose election changes.
description_long: The Independent’s August 2026 account described multiple administration efforts to expand federal influence over election administration and the legal and political obstacles they encountered before the midterms. It reported that the Justice Department had lost more than 20 cases seeking state voter data and that federal courts had blocked executive orders aimed at creating a national voter registration list and restricting mail ballots. The Supreme Court had not yet resolved the administration’s requests concerning vote-by-mail, while Congress had not reached agreement on the SAVE America Act. The article also recounted Trump’s response to a media host who floated declaring a national emergency to impose voter ID measures: Trump said, “stranger things have happened.” That was an open-ended remark, not an announcement that an emergency had been declared. The account further described a judge blocking a subpoena for personal information about Fulton County election workers and the removal of three remaining members of the Election Assistance Commission. The reported court rulings were concrete limits on these efforts; proposed emergency or military actions remained possibilities discussed in the article, not completed operations.
